3D Skew-Normal Splatting

Xiangru Wu Affiliation: Fudan University Email: xiangruwu22@m.fudan.edu.cn    Ke Fan Affiliation: Fudan University Email: kfan21@m.fudan.edu.cn    Yanwei Fu Affiliation: Fudan University Email: yanweifu@fudan.edu.cn
Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a leading representation for real-time novel view synthesis and has been widely adopted in various downstream applications. The core strength of 3DGS lies in its efficient kernel-based scene representation, where Gaussian primitives provide favorable mathematical and computational properties. However, under a finite primitive budget, the symmetric shape of each primitive directly affects representation compactness, especially near asymmetric structures such as object boundaries and one-sided surfaces. Recent works have explored more complex kernel distributions; however, they either remain within the elliptical family or rely on hard truncation, which limits continuous shape control and introduces distributional discontinuities. In this paper, we propose Skew-Normal Splatting (SNS), which adopts the Azzalini Skew-Normal distribution as the fundamental primitive. By introducing a learnable and bounded skewness parameter, SNS can continuously interpolate between symmetric Gaussians and Half-Gaussian-like shapes, enabling flexible modeling of both sharp boundaries and interior regions. Moreover, SNS preserves analytical tractability under affine transformations and marginalization. This property allows seamless integration into existing Gaussian Splatting rasterization pipelines. Furthermore, to address the strong coupling between scale, rotation, and skewness parameters, we introduce a decoupled parameterization and a block-wise optimization strategy to enhance training stability and accuracy. Extensive experiments on standard novel-view synthesis benchmarks show that SNS consistently improves reconstruction quality over Gaussian and recent non-Gaussian kernels, with clearer benefits on sharp boundaries and thin or one-sided structures.

1 Introduction

In the field of novel view synthesis, the increasing demand for real-time interactivity has exposed the limitations of traditional NeRF-based Mildenhall et al. (2020); Mildenhall et al. (2022); Barron et al. (2021); Barron et al. (2022) methods regarding rendering efficiency and training overhead. Since its introduction, 3D Gaussian Splatting Kerbl et al. (2023) has rapidly emerged as a dominant alternative to early NeRF approaches. By leveraging explicit scene representations and fast, differentiable rendering, it achieves a superior balance between visual fidelity and computational performance and has been widely used in fields such as robotics Keetha et al. (2024), autonomous driving Zhou et al. (2024), and cultural heritage preservation Dahaghin et al. (2024). The success of 3D Gaussian Splatting is attributed to its use of Gaussian functions as kernels, which provide powerful approximation capabilities alongside mathematical and computational efficiency Zwicker et al. (2001); Zwicker et al. (2002). Nevertheless, the universal approximation property of kernel-based methods remains largely a theoretical guarantee, typically predicated on the availability of an infinite and sufficiently dense distribution of kernels. In the practical regime of a finite primitive budget, the distributional form of each kernel directly dictates representation compactness and reconstruction accuracy. Symmetric Gaussian kernels often require multiple overlapping primitives to approximate sharp boundaries, leading to redundant representations and blurred reconstructions.

Recent efforts Zhu et al. (2025); Li et al. (2025); Hamdi et al. (2024) have investigated the use of more sophisticated distributions as alternatives to the standard Gaussian. Despite some success, these methods still have limitations. Both Generalized Exponential Splatting (GES) Hamdi et al. (2024) and Student Splatting and Scooping (SSS) Zhu et al. (2025) propose to extend the Gaussian primitive by modifying the radial density post-whitening; however, such methods are still restricted to the elliptical distribution family, which imposes a persistent radial symmetry on the representation. Among these efforts, HGS Li et al. (2025) adopts the Half-Gaussian distribution, representing an early attempt to introduce asymmetric kernels into scene modeling. However, this approach relies on a hard truncation scheme that simply divides a Gaussian distribution at its centroid, thereby offering only limited expressivity in terms of skewness. Furthermore, such truncation inherently introduces discontinuities into the primitive’s distribution.

To further characterize the asymmetry that is prevalent in real data, many works in Statistics Kundu (2014); Elal-Olivero (2010); Mameli and Musio (2011); Mudholkar and Hutson (2000); Arellano-Valle and Azzalini (2006); Arnold and Beaver (2000) extend the Gaussian distribution with additional shape parameters to capture skewness. These distributions are widely used in fields such as economics and finance, biomedicine, and spatial statistics Vernic (2006); Carmichael and Coën (2013); Frühwirth-Schnatter and Pyne (2010); Rimstad and Omre (2014); Zhang and El-Shaarawi (2010). Among these works, Azzalini’s Skew-Normal distribution Azzalini and Capitanio (1999) is widely regarded as a classical extension of the Gaussian distribution, due to its simplicity and clear probabilistic construction, providing a useful reference for our work.

To this end, we propose Skew-Normal Splatting (SNS), which employs the Skew-Normal distribution of Azzalini as the underlying primitive for scene modeling. By subsuming the standard Gaussian and half-Gaussian distributions as special or limiting cases, the Skew-Normal distribution provides a continuous and tunable mechanism for asymmetric modeling. On one hand, it offers the flexibility to capture non-symmetric structures such as sharp edges and corners; on the other, it maintains the capacity to effectively represent the interior regions of objects. As Fig. 1 shows, we fit the same 1D square wave using Gaussian, Skew-Normal, and Half-Gaussian kernels, respectively. For a fair comparison, all methods are restricted to 4 components and optimized via gradient descent. The Gaussian model exhibits boundary ringing-like artifacts, including overshoot and undershoot near step transitions. The Half-Gaussian method offers a marginal improvement but introduces discontinuities and sharp peaks at the step changes. In contrast, SNS can effectively fit both sharp edges and flat portions of the square wave, demonstrating its superior representational capacity.

Furthermore, the SNS remains analytically tractable under affine transformations and marginalization. Leveraging this mathematical convenience, we re-derive the projection and integration routines required to incorporate SNS into the splat-based rasterization pipeline, thereby enabling highly efficient computation.

Beyond its representational benefits, the transition to asymmetric primitives introduces new analytical and optimization challenges. We observe that the location parameter of a Skew-Normal distribution does not coincide with its spatial mean. We thus derive a corrected operational center to ensure accurate bounding-box localization. Furthermore, to resolve the optimization instability caused by the coupling between orientation and skewness, we introduce a decoupled parameterization in the primitive’s canonical coordinate system, supported by a block-wise alternating update strategy. This design effectively reduces parameter interference, ensuring stable convergence and improved generalization. Formally, our contributions include:

  • •

    We introduce Azzalini’s Skew-Normal distribution to Gaussian Splatting, which has varying degrees of skewness for 3D scene modeling and can simultaneously handle object boundaries and interiors.

  • •

    We derive a complete analytical framework for Skew-Normal kernels, including closed-form affine projection, corrected footprint localization, and efficient gradient computation for rasterization, preserving compatibility with existing 3DGS pipelines.

  • •

    We identify the optimization coupling between geometric and skewness parameters and propose a decoupled reparameterization along with a block-wise alternating update scheme to enhance training stability.

  • •

    SNS achieves consistent PSNR gains over recent non-Gaussian variants and improves visual preservation of sharp structures and object completeness.

2 Related Work

NeRF methods. Early approaches to 3D reconstruction such as SfM Schönberger and Frahm (2016); Wei et al. (2020) and MVS Yao et al. (2018); Cao et al. (2022) typically rely on explicit geometric estimation. Recently, Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) Mildenhall et al. (2020); Mildenhall et al. (2022) implicitly learn scene geometry and appearance by parameterizing volumetric density and color through neural networks, utilizing volume rendering to synthesize novel views. Mip-NeRF Barron et al. (2021) and Mip-NeRF 360 Barron et al. (2022) reduce aliasing and extend NeRF to unbounded scenes, while explicit or hybrid representations such as Plenoxels Fridovich-Keil et al. (2022) and K-Planes Fridovich-Keil et al. (2023) improve training and rendering efficiency. Beyond reconstruction, NeRF has been extended to sparse-view synthesis Yu et al. (2021); Wang et al. (2021b), object-centric decomposition Yu et al. (2022); Qi et al. (2023), neural surface reconstruction Yariv et al. (2021); Wang et al. (2021a), and dynamic scene modeling Pumarola et al. (2021); Park et al. (2021), substantially advancing neural 3D representations. Despite their strong rendering quality, NeRF-based methods typically rely on dense ray sampling and implicit network evaluation, which makes training and rendering computationally expensive compared with explicit splatting-based representations.

Splatting methods. The 3DGS Kerbl et al. (2023) models the scene with optimizable Gaussian elements and projects them onto the image plane through an efficient splatting rasterizer, thereby significantly accelerating the rendering process. Building upon this paradigm, several works have improved 3DGS across multiple dimensions. Mip-Splatting Yu et al. (2024) focuses on anti-aliasing and multi-scale rendering, while Scaffold-GS Lu et al. (2024) and Octree-GS Ren et al. (2025) introduce hierarchical structures to enhance representation efficiency. To optimize the growth and pruning strategies of Gaussian primitives, Pixel-GS Zhang et al. (2024b) and AbsGS Ye et al. (2024b) refine the density control mechanisms. Furthermore, 3DGS has been extended to a broader range of applications: GaussianEditor Wang et al. (2024); Chen et al. (2024) enables scene editing within the Gaussian representation, and 4DGS Wu et al. (2024a); Yang et al. (2024) further generalizes the framework to dynamic scene modeling. Collectively, these advancements have established 3DGS as a powerful alternative for efficient 3D scene representation and rendering. Beyond these domains, the framework has also been applied to 3D content generation Tang et al. (2024b); Yi et al. (2024); Tang et al. (2024a); Xu et al. (2024), language-driven scene understanding Wu et al. (2024b); Qin et al. (2024); Guo et al. (2026), and 3D scene segmentation Cen et al. (2025); Ye et al. (2024a). More recently, several works have explored extending 3DGS by modifying the underlying kernel functions of the Gaussian primitives. For instance, GES Hamdi et al. (2024) adopts the Generalized Exponential Function, while SSS employs the Student’s t-distribution Zhu et al. (2025). Pushing this further, 3D-HGS Li et al. (2025) introduces the half-Gaussian distribution to facilitate the representation of more irregular primitives. Unlike GES and SSS, which modify the radial profile after whitening and therefore remain largely symmetric in canonical space, our SNS introduces directional skewness as an intrinsic primitive parameter. Unlike 3D-HGS, SNS avoids hard truncation and provides a continuous path from Gaussian-like to half-Gaussian-like shapes.

3 Method

3.1 Gaussian Splatting

Scene Representation. 3DGS models the scene using 3D Gaussian kernels. Each kernel is parameterized by a center position μ∈ℝ3\mu\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, a 3D covariance matrix Σ∈ℝ3×3\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}, an opacity value o∈[0,1]o\in[0,1], and view-dependent color features cc. To ensure positive semi-definiteness during optimization, Σ\Sigma is factorized into a scaling matrix S∈ℝ3×3S\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3} and a rotation matrix R∈ℝ3×3R\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}, formulated as: Σ=R​S​S⊤​R⊤\Sigma=RSS^{\top}R^{\top}. These 3D Gaussians are projected onto the 2D screen space to render images. Given a viewing transformation matrix WW and the Jacobian of the affine projection approximation JJ, the 2D covariance matrix, denoted by Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}, can be computed as: Σ′=J​W​Σ​W⊤​J⊤\Sigma^{\prime}=JW\Sigma W^{\top}J^{\top}.

Volumetric Alpha-Blending. The rendering process evaluates the final color C⁡(u)C(u) at pixel uu through a tile-based rasterizer. Analogous to volumetric rendering, 3DGS performs alpha-blending by sorting the projected Gaussians along the ray corresponding to the pixel from front to back. For a set of 𝒩\mathcal{N} ordered, intersecting Gaussians, the pixel color is aggregated as Kerbl et al. (2023):

C⁡(u)=∑i=1𝒩ci​ai​(u)​∏j=1i−1(1−aj​(u)),C(u)=\sum_{i=1}^{\mathcal{N}}c_{i}a_{i}(u)\prod_{j=1}^{i-1}\left(1-a_{j}(u)\right), (1)

where cic_{i} is the color evaluated from the SH coefficients. The term ai​(u)a_{i}(u) denotes the spatial influence of the ii-th Gaussian evaluated at pixel uu, which is obtained by multiplying the learned opacity oio_{i} with the 2D Gaussian kernel:

ai​(u)=oi​exp⁡(−12​(u−μ^i)⊤​Σ^i−1​(u−μ^i)),a_{i}(u)=o_{i}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(u-\hat{\mu}_{i})^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{i}^{-1}(u-\hat{\mu}_{i})\right), (2)

where μ^i\hat{\mu}_{i} is the projected 2D center position.

3.2 3D Skew-Normal Kernel

We inherit Azzalini’s definition of the Skew-Normal Distribution (SND), which provides directional asymmetry through a new parameter α\alpha. A d-dimensional SND random variable YY is denoted as Y∼𝒮​𝒩d​(μ,Ω,α)Y\sim\mathcal{SN}_{d}(\mu,\Omega,\alpha), where the parameters are called location, scale matrix, and slant Azzalini and Capitanio (1999), respectively. The slant parameter α\alpha is highly coupled with Ω\Omega. When α\alpha is kept fixed, applying a spatial rotation to the model does not only reorient the primitive but also changes its intrinsic geometric shape. To decouple the shape from the orientation, we propose an unnormalized and reparameterized 3D Skew-Normal kernel, which is defined by a location vector μ∈ℝ3\mu\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, a scale matrix Ω=R​S​S⊤​R⊤∈ℝ3×3\Omega=RSS^{\top}R^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}, and a learnable latent variable k∈ℝ3k\in\mathbb{R}^{3}:

S​N​(x,μ,Ω,k)=G3​(x−μ,Ω)​Φ​(α⊤​ω−1​(x−μ)),SN(x;\mu,\Omega,k)=G_{3}(x-\mu;\Omega)\,\Phi\left(\alpha^{\top}\omega^{-1}(x-\mu)\right), (3)

where α=ω​R​S−1​k\alpha=\omega RS^{-1}k, ω=(Ω⊙𝐈3)1/2\omega=\left(\Omega\odot\mathbf{I}_{3}\right)^{1/2}, G3​(x−μ,Ω)=exp⁡(−12​(x−μ)⊤​Ω−1​(x−μ))G_{3}(x-\mu;\Omega)=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(x-\mu)^{\top}\Omega^{-1}(x-\mu)\right), and Φ⁡(⋅)\Phi(\cdot) denotes the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the standard univariate normal distribution. The symbol ⊙\odot refers to the Hadamard product. This formulation provides four main advantages:

Continuous Shape Interpolation. The Skew-Normal distribution includes the Gaussian and half-Gaussian as limiting cases, providing a natural continuum between symmetric and maximally skewed geometries. It reduces to a Gaussian ellipsoid when α=𝟎\alpha=\mathbf{0}, and approaches a half-ellipsoid as ‖α‖→∞\|\alpha\|\to\infty. As illustrated in Fig. 3, this continuous interpolation enables a single kernel to represent a broad spectrum of geometric structures. By increasing the magnitude from ‖k1‖≈2.24\|k_{1}\|\approx 2.24 to 4​‖k1‖≈8.944\|k_{1}\|\approx 8.94, the kernel reshapes into a sharp half-ellipsoid. Crucially, further scaling to 20​‖k1‖20\|k_{1}\| yields a slight visual change, demonstrating that the skewness converges rapidly to its limiting form. Such flexibility extends the expressive power of Gaussian kernels while preserving a compact and principled parameterization.

Bounded Skewness. The shape of the SND is influenced by the slant α\alpha and the scale matrix Ω\Omega. To provide a single, scalar measure of skewness, Mardia’s measure of skewness Azzalini and Capitanio (1999) is expressed as:

γ1,dM=(4−π2)2​((2/π)​α∗21+(1−2/π)​α∗2)3,\gamma_{1,d}^{M}=\left(\frac{4-\pi}{2}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{(2/\pi)\alpha_{*}^{2}}{1+(1-2/\pi)\alpha_{*}^{2}}\right)^{3}, (4)

where α∗=(α⊤​Ω¯​α)12∈[0,∞)\alpha_{*}=\left(\alpha^{\top}\bar{\Omega}\alpha\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\in\left[0,\infty\right). As shown in Eq.(4), γ1,dM\gamma_{1,d}^{M} is monotonically increasing with respect to α∗\alpha_{*}. When α∗=0\alpha_{*}=0, γ1,dM=0\gamma_{1,d}^{M}=0; when α∗→∞\alpha_{*}\to\infty, γ1,d→2​(π−4)2(π−2)3\gamma_{1,d}\to\frac{2(\pi-4)^{2}}{(\pi-2)^{3}}, which is approximately 0.990670.99067. Therefore, the skewness of the SND is confined to a bounded region, preventing the distribution from being excessively stretched. This bounded property is important for the 3DGS framework. 3DGS relies on tile-based rasterization, which requires primitives to have a spatially compact footprint for efficient bounding box calculation. An unbounded asymmetric tail would cause a primitive to intersect with an excessive number of tiles, degrading rendering performance. On the other hand, the local affine approximation (via Jacobian JJ) employed in 3DGS is fundamentally predicated on a localized spatial footprint. An arbitrarily extended tail would violate this assumption and lead to instability during optimization.

Decoupled Skewness Measure. By defining the slant parameter as α=ω​R​S−1​k\alpha=\omega RS^{-1}k, we decouple the asymmetry of the distribution from its affine transformation components (i.e., RR and SS). Under this reparameterization, the term α∗\alpha_{*} in Eq.(4) reduces to the L2L_{2}-norm of the skew vector kk, implying that γ1,dM\gamma_{1,d}^{M} is solely determined by ‖k‖2\|k\|_{2}. It reveals that the magnitude of kk comprehensively encapsulates the departure from normality. In Fig. 3, panels (b) and (c) share the same k1k_{1} but differ in rotation RR. The resulting density in (c) is a rigid rotation of (b), verifying that kk is an intrinsic property defined in the primitive’s canonical coordinate system; varying RR only alters global orientation without deforming the asymmetric kernel itself. Additionally, shifting kk’s orientation (e.g., rotating k1=(2,−1)⊤k_{1}=(2,-1)^{\top} to k2k_{2} while maintaining ‖k1‖=‖k2‖\|k_{1}\|=\|k_{2}\|) dictates the specific axis of the skew, remapping the kernel’s asymmetry to a new direction.

Closed-form 2D Projection. The SND is closed under affine transformations. We derive the analytical form by projecting a 3D primitive to the 2D image plane. This derivation requires an affine transformation matrix A=J​W∈ℝ2×3A=JW\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 3}. Formally, a 2D Skew-Normal kernel is described by:

S​N2​D​(u,μ2​D,Ω2​D,m2​D)=G2​(u−μ2​D,Ω2​D)​Φ​((m2​D)⊤​(u−μ2​D)).SN^{2D}(u;\mu^{2D},\Omega^{2D},m^{2D})=G_{2}(u-\mu^{2D};\Omega^{2D})\,\Phi\left((m^{2D})^{\top}(u-\mu^{2D})\right). (5)

where u∈ℝ2u\in\mathbb{R}^{2} denotes the pixel coordinate,

μ2​D\displaystyle\mu^{2D} =Aμ,Ω2​D=AΩA⊤,\displaystyle=A\mu,\quad\Omega^{2D}=A\Omega A^{\top}, (6)
m2​D\displaystyle m^{2D} =(Ω2​D)−1​A​R​S​k1+k⊤​k−(A​R​S​k)⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​A​R​S​k.\displaystyle=\frac{(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}ARSk}{\sqrt{1+k^{\top}k-(ARSk)^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}ARSk}}.

The reparameterization of α\alpha is essential; otherwise, the diagonal matrix ω\omega remains coupled with the inverse 2D covariance, which complicates gradient backpropagation. Although the reparameterized expression for m2​Dm^{2D} appears computationally heavy, we reduce the training cost by restructuring the backward propagation paths through algebraic reductions. Details are in appendix  A.1 and  B.

3.3 Forward Modeling of Splatting

Restricting primitives strictly to a positive density space bounds their representational capacity. Following SSS, we allow signed opacity values oi∈[−1,1]o_{i}\in[-1,1], enabling primitives to both contribute color and subtract volumetric density from the scene. This subtractive capability can represent complex topologies with fewer kernels. At a pixel uu, the front-to-back alpha blending evaluates as:

C⁡(u)=∑i∈𝒩ci​oi​S​Ni2​D​(u)​∏j=1i−1(1−oj​S​Nj2​D​(u)),C(u)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{N}}c_{i}o_{i}SN^{2D}_{i}(u)\prod_{j=1}^{i-1}\left(1-o_{j}SN^{2D}_{j}(u)\right), (7)

where 𝒩\mathcal{N} is the depth-sorted set of intersecting kernels.

Traditional splatting frameworks, such as 3DGS and SSS, anchor their tile-based bounding boxes to the nominal location parameter μ2​D\mu^{2D}, which is the mean of the distribution. As shown in Fig. 3, μ2​D\mu^{2D} deviates from the spatial mean because the slant parameter α\alpha shifts the probability mass. Relying on μ2​D\mu^{2D} for bounding boxes localization is ineffective in capturing the spatial density of skewed objects. To address this, we physically shift the 2D footprint to the true spatial mean, deriving the corrected operational center, μb​b​o​x\mu_{bbox}, as a deterministic spatial offset:

μb​b​o​x=μ2​D+2π⋅A​R​S​k1+k⊤​k.\mu_{bbox}=\mu^{2D}+\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\cdot\frac{ARSk}{\sqrt{1+k^{\top}k}}. (8)

3.4 Stable Optimization via Parameter Decoupling

Optimizing Skew-Normal kernels is particularly challenging due to the coupling between the geometric and skewness parameters. We update the positional parameters μ\mu using Stochastic Gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (SGHMC) Zhu et al. (2025), which introduces stochasticity to help the model escape local minima. The greater challenge, however, comes from the slant parameter α\alpha, as it deeply couples the rotation RR, scaling SS, and the latent variable kk. We decouple them from two perspectives:

Internal parameter dependencies. As in Sec. 3.2, the magnitude of parameter kk explicitly determines the skewness. We therefore factorize kk into an independent magnitude scalar mk∈ℝ+m_{k}\in\mathbb{R}_{+} and a direction vector dk∈ℝ3​(‖dk‖2=1)d_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}(\|d_{k}\|_{2}=1). We further parametrize the magnitude and direction as:

mk=81+e​x​p​(−x6),dk=v‖v‖2+ϵ,m_{k}=\frac{8}{1+exp(-\frac{x}{6})},\quad d_{k}=\frac{v}{\|v\|_{2}+\epsilon}, (9)

where x∈ℝ,v∈ℝ3x\in\mathbb{R},v\in\mathbb{R}^{3}. This structural decomposition isolates the skew direction and skew intensity, allowing the model to optimize them independently.

Inter-parameter interference. Although decomposing kk into magnitude and direction improves stability, updating shape parameters (R,S,mk,dk)(R,S,m_{k},d_{k}) simultaneously still leads to suboptimal convergence. Specifically, adjustments to the base ellipsoid’s orientation frequently conflict with the skew direction. To address this, we divide the training process into two phases. First, all parameters (R,S,mk,dkR,S,m_{k},d_{k}) are jointly optimized using standard Adam to establish a reasonable global structure. In the second phase, a Block Coordinate Descent (BCD) strategy is activated. The optimization follows a cyclic alternating schedule: in the first part of each cycle, the ellipsoidal base parameters (R,SR,S) are updated while the skew parameters (mk,dkm_{k},d_{k}) are frozen; in the second part, (mk,dkm_{k},d_{k}) are refined while (R,SR,S) are held constant.

While SGHMC is utilized for the positional parameters μ\mu, the Adam optimizer is employed for all remaining variables. SGHMC naturally provides stochastic global search, preventing positional parameters from collapsing into local minima. Meanwhile, the alternating update scheme governs the shape parameters, ensuring geometric stability throughout training.

4 Experiments

Datasets and Metrics. We evaluate SNS on 11 scenes across 3 datasets to validate our contributions: 7 scenes from Mip-NeRF 360 Barron et al. (2022), 2 scenes from Tanks & Temples Knapitsch et al. (2017), and 2 scenes from Deep Blending Hedman et al. (2018). Following the standard evaluation metrics, we employ three metrics: Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM), and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS). We report dataset-level averages, with per-scene results in the appendix.

Baselines. (1) kernel-level variants such as GES Hamdi et al. (2024), 3D-HGS Li et al. (2025) and SSS Zhu et al. (2025), which introduce non-Gaussian primitives; (2) optimization-focused methods like Scaffold-GS Lu et al. (2024), Fre-GS Zhang et al. (2024a) and 3DGS-MCMC Kheradmand et al. (2024); and (3) Neural Radiance Field method such as Mip-NeRF Barron et al. (2021). For a fair comparison, we use the results either from original papers or run publicly available implementations under the same settings.

Implementation Details. Our model is implemented in PyTorch, with the core rasterization engine extended from the 3DGS framework to support the asymmetric 2D Skew-Normal kernel. All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs. In terms of computational efficiency, SNS demonstrates a training overhead comparable to SSS; for instance, in the drjohnson scene, SNS completes 30,000 iterations in 38m 4s (29.89 dB PSNR), while SSS requires 38m 7s (29.66 dB PSNR) on the same test set.

4.1 Results

Performance Comparison.

We report the quantitative comparison of our method with state-of-the-art methods in Tab. 1. Overall, our method achieves the best or highly competitive results across all datasets and metrics, validating the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed approach. Our method showed the most consistent and strongest performance on PSNR, achieving 30.17 on Mip-NeRF360, 25.08 on Tanks&Temples, and 30.30 on Deep Blending. The improvement is most notable on Tanks&Temples. Compared with SSS, the strongest baseline, our method achieves higher PSNR (24.87→\rightarrow25.08) and SSIM (0.873→\rightarrow0.877), and lower LPIPS (0.138→\rightarrow0.132) on Tanks&Temples. SNS remains highly competitive on SSIM for Mip-NeRF360 and LPIPS for Deep Blending, achieving results nearly on par with the best-performing methods.

Qualitative Results. Our method demonstrates better object completeness across multiple scenes in Fig.  4. For locally complex objects, such as the curtain above the window in the room scene and the tower-shaped structure in the train scene, our method maintains the complete structure and clear boundaries. In contrast, SSS and 3DGS-MCMC exhibit noticeable missing regions in the train scene, while GS and 3DHGS produce holes and fuzzy boundaries in the room scene.

In terms of texture clarity, our method more effectively preserves high-frequency details. For example, the wavy stripes on top of the transparent plastic box in the bonsai scene, the texture and shadows on the cloth behind the chair in the kitchen scene, and the distant trees in the train scene are all reconstructed and rendered with clearer details. By contrast, the original GS produces over-smoothed reconstructions in texture-rich regions, leading to noticeable blur. Besides, in the drjohnson scene, SNS exhibits the mildest artifacts among all compared methods. These results show that our method better handles complex regions in novel view synthesis.

Different kernels comparison. Table 2 provides the detailed PSNR scores evaluated with GS, GES, HGS, SSS, and our SNS. In this comparison, we treat standard 3DGS as the baseline. Across all scenes, SNS outperforms all other models by at least 0.1 dB. For example, our method outperforms SSS by 0.45 dB on the Room scene, 0.29 dB on the Train scene, and 0.24 dB on the Playroom scene. Overall, our SN formulation consistently delivers the best performance across all tested 3D scenes.

4.2 Ablations

Table  3 details the ablation study on individual module contributions. Using the vanilla Skew-Normal distribution as our baseline, we compare three configurations: (1) kk-decomposition: Decomposes the skew vector kk into magnitude and direction, without alternating optimization. (2) Alternating optimization: Alternately optimizes (R,S)(R,S) and kk, without kk-decomposition. (3) Full model: Incorporates both kk-decomposition and alternating optimization. Full experimental results are available in Appendix C.

Both modules contribute to the final performance through distinct mechanisms. Alternating optimization yields consistent improvements in pixel-level reconstruction, increasing mean PSNR from 30.0630.06 to 30.1430.14 on Mip-NeRF 360 and from 30.1630.16 to 30.3030.30 on Deep Blending. This indicates that alternating updates for (R,S)(R,S) and kk effectively decouple geometric parameters from skew parameters, stabilizing the optimization process. Meanwhile, kk-decomposition consistently enhances SSIM and LPIPS across all datasets, suggesting that decomposing the skew vector into magnitude and direction provides a superior parameterization that improves optimization dynamics. The full model delivers the most significant gains in PSNR, while maintaining highly competitive LPIPS and SSIM performance across scenes. Thus, these results suggest that the two optimization components provide complementary but moderate gains. The full model achieves the best average PSNR across all datasets, while individual variants may slightly outperform it on perceptual metrics in some cases, indicating that the modules mainly improve reconstruction fidelity and stability rather than uniformly optimizing every metric.

5 Conclusion

We propose Skew-Normal Splatting, which introduces controllable skewness into Gaussian Splatting to better represent asymmetric geometries, sharp boundaries, and one-sided structures. SNS preserves analytical projection for efficient splatting and further improves optimization stability through decoupled parameterization and block-wise updates. Experiments show consistent improvements over existing Gaussian and non-Gaussian kernels.

Appendix

Appendix A Mathematical Proof

In the implementation of SNS, the kernel is defined using the unnormalized probability density function (PDF) of the Skew-Normal distribution. Although this differs from the standard Skew-Normal (SN) distribution by a normalization coefficient, they share identical properties regarding affine transformations and geometric characteristics. For clarity and convenience, the following derivations are conducted within the framework of the standard SN distribution.

A.1 Closure under Affine Transformations

Let X∼S​Nd​(μ,Ω,α)X\sim SN_{d}(\mu,\Omega,\alpha) be a dd-dimensional Skew-Normal random variable. Its stochastic representation Azzalini and Capitanio (1999) is given by:

X=μ+ωZ∣U>0,(UZ)∼N1+d(𝟎,(1δ⊤δΩ¯)),X=\mu+\omega Z\mid U>0,\quad\begin{pmatrix}U\\ Z\end{pmatrix}\sim N_{1+d}\!\left(\mathbf{0},\begin{pmatrix}1&\delta^{\top}\\ \delta&\bar{\Omega}\end{pmatrix}\right), (10)

where ω=(Ω⊙𝐈d)1/2\omega=\left(\Omega\odot\mathbf{I}_{d}\right)^{1/2}, Ω¯=ω−1​Ω​ω−1\bar{\Omega}=\omega^{-1}\Omega\omega^{-1}, and δ=Ω¯​α1+α⊤​Ω¯​α\delta=\frac{\bar{\Omega}\alpha}{\sqrt{1+\alpha^{\top}\bar{\Omega}\alpha}}.

Consider an affine transformation Y=T​X+bY=TX+b, where T∈ℝh×dT\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times d}, rank​(T)=h≤d\text{rank}(T)=h\leq d and b∈ℝhb\in\mathbb{R}^{h}. Substituting the representation of XX yields: Y=(T​μ+b)+T​ω​Z|U>0Y=(T\mu+b)+T\omega Z\mid U>0.

To show that YY is also Skew-Normal, we express it in the standard stochastic representation. Let μY=T​μ+b\mu_{Y}=T\mu+b and W=T​ω​ZW=T\omega Z. Since (U,Z⊤)⊤(U,Z^{\top})^{\top} is multivariate normal, the joint distribution of (U,W⊤)⊤(U,W^{\top})^{\top} remains normal with zero mean. The variance of WW and the covariance between UU and WW are given by:

Var​(W)=ΩY=T​ω​Ω¯​ω​T⊤=T​Ω​T⊤,\displaystyle\text{Var}(W)=\Omega_{Y}=T\omega\bar{\Omega}\omega T^{\top}=T\Omega T^{\top}, (11)
Cov​(U,W)=Cov​(U,Z)​ω​T⊤=δ⊤​ω​T⊤.\displaystyle\text{Cov}(U,W)=\text{Cov}(U,Z)\omega T^{\top}=\delta^{\top}\omega T^{\top}.

Defining ωY=(ΩY⊙𝐈h)1/2\omega_{Y}=\left(\Omega_{Y}\odot\mathbf{I}_{h}\right)^{1/2} and ZY=ωY−1​WZ_{Y}=\omega_{Y}^{-1}W, we can rewrite Y=μY+ωY​ZY|U>0Y=\mu_{Y}+\omega_{Y}Z_{Y}\mid U>0, while Var​(ZY)=ωY−1​ΩY​ωY−1=Ω¯Y\text{Var}(Z_{Y})=\omega_{Y}^{-1}\Omega_{Y}\omega_{Y}^{-1}=\bar{\Omega}_{Y}, and Cov​(U,ZY)=Cov​(U,W)​ωY−1=δ⊤​ω​T⊤​ωY−1\text{Cov}(U,Z_{Y})=\text{Cov}(U,W)\omega_{Y}^{-1}=\delta^{\top}\omega T^{\top}\omega_{Y}^{-1}. Letting δY=ωY−1​T​ω​δ\delta_{Y}=\omega_{Y}^{-1}T\omega\delta, we finally obtain the required block-covariance structure:

Y=μY+ωYZY∣U>0,(UZY)∼N1+h(𝟎,(1δY⊤δYΩ¯Y)).Y=\mu_{Y}+\omega_{Y}Z_{Y}\mid U>0,\quad\begin{pmatrix}U\\ Z_{Y}\end{pmatrix}\sim N_{1+h}\!\left(\mathbf{0},\begin{pmatrix}1&\delta_{Y}^{\top}\\ \delta_{Y}&\bar{\Omega}_{Y}\end{pmatrix}\right). (12)

Since the conditioning event U>0U>0 is unchanged and (U,ZY⊤)⊤(U,Z_{Y}^{\top})^{\top} satisfies the standard joint normal structure, we conclude that YY follows an hh-dimensional SND.

A.2 2D Kernel Parameters

Let X∼SN3​(μ,Ω,α)X\sim\text{SN}_{3}(\mu,\Omega,\alpha) represent the 3D Skew-Normal kernel, and consider a linear projection: Y=A​XY=AX, where A∈ℝ2×3A\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 3}. Building upon the property derived in A.1, we can simply write Y∼S​N2​(μY,ΩY,αY)Y\sim SN_{2}(\mu_{Y},\Omega_{Y},\alpha_{Y}), with μY=A​μ\mu_{Y}=A\mu, ΩY=A​Ω​A⊤\Omega_{Y}=A\Omega A^{\top}, and δY=ωY−1​A​ω​δ\delta_{Y}=\omega_{Y}^{-1}A\omega\delta.

Recall that δY=Ω¯Y​αY1+αY⊤​Ω¯Y​αY\delta_{Y}=\frac{\bar{\Omega}_{Y}\alpha_{Y}}{\sqrt{1+\alpha_{Y}^{\top}\bar{\Omega}_{Y}\alpha_{Y}}} and 1−δY⊤​Ω¯Y−1​δY=11+αY⊤​Ω¯Y​αY1-\delta_{Y}^{\top}\bar{\Omega}_{Y}^{-1}\delta_{Y}=\frac{1}{1+\alpha_{Y}^{\top}\bar{\Omega}_{Y}\alpha_{Y}}. We can write:

αY=1+αY⊤​Ω¯Y​αY⋅Ω¯Y−1​δY=Ω¯Y−1​δY1−δY⊤​Ω¯Y−1​δY=ωY​ΩY−1​A​ω​δ1−(A​ω​δ)⊤​ΩY−1​A​ω​δ,\displaystyle\alpha_{Y}=\sqrt{1+\alpha_{Y}^{\top}\bar{\Omega}_{Y}\alpha_{Y}}\cdot\bar{\Omega}_{Y}^{-1}\delta_{Y}=\frac{\bar{\Omega}_{Y}^{-1}\delta_{Y}}{\sqrt{1-\delta_{Y}^{\top}\bar{\Omega}_{Y}^{-1}\delta_{Y}}}=\frac{\omega_{Y}\Omega_{Y}^{-1}A\omega\delta}{\sqrt{1-(A\omega\delta)^{\top}\Omega_{Y}^{-1}A\omega\delta}}, (13)

where ωY=(ΩY⊙𝐈2)1/2\omega_{Y}=(\Omega_{Y}\odot\mathbf{I}_{2})^{1/2}, ω=(Ω⊙𝐈3)1/2\omega=(\Omega\odot\mathbf{I}_{3})^{1/2}, and δ=Ω¯​α1+α⊤​Ω¯​α\delta=\frac{\bar{\Omega}\alpha}{\sqrt{1+\alpha^{\top}\bar{\Omega}\alpha}}.

In our formulation, α\alpha is explicitly parameterized as α=ω​R​S−1​k\alpha=\omega RS^{-1}k, where Ω=R​S​S⊤​R⊤\Omega=RSS^{\top}R^{\top}. Substituting this structural definition into the equations above simplifies the expressions:

ω​δ\displaystyle\omega\delta =ω​Ω¯​ω​R​S−1​k1+k⊤​S−1​R⊤​ω​Ω¯​ω​R​S−1​k=Ω​R​S−1​k1+k⊤​S−1​R⊤​Ω​R​S−1​k\displaystyle=\frac{\omega\bar{\Omega}\omega RS^{-1}k}{\sqrt{1+k^{\top}S^{-1}R^{\top}\omega\bar{\Omega}\omega RS^{-1}k}}=\frac{\Omega RS^{-1}k}{\sqrt{1+k^{\top}S^{-1}R^{\top}\Omega RS^{-1}k}} (14)
=R​S​S⊤​R⊤​R​S−1​k1+k⊤​S−1​R⊤​R​S​S⊤​R⊤​R​S−1​k=R​S​k1+k⊤​k.\displaystyle=\frac{RSS^{\top}R^{\top}RS^{-1}k}{\sqrt{1+k^{\top}S^{-1}R^{\top}RSS^{\top}R^{\top}RS^{-1}k}}=\frac{RSk}{\sqrt{1+k^{\top}k}}.

Applying the transformation Eq.(14) to Eq.(13) gives:

αY=ωY​ΩY−1​A​R​S​k1+k⊤​k−(A​R​S​k)⊤​(ΩY)−1​A​R​S​k.\alpha_{Y}=\frac{\omega_{Y}\Omega_{Y}^{-1}ARSk}{\sqrt{1+k^{\top}k-(ARSk)^{\top}(\Omega_{Y})^{-1}ARSk}}. (15)

A.3 The Mean of the Skew-Normal Distribution

Unlike the multivariate normal distribution, the location parameter μ\mu of X∼S​Nd​(μ,Ω,α)X\sim SN_{d}(\mu,\Omega,\alpha) does not equal its exact mean. The true mean, 𝔼⁡[X]\mathbb{E}[X], can be analytically derived using the stochastic representation introduced in Eq.(10). Taking the expectation of X=μ+ω​Z|U>0X=\mu+\omega Z\mid U>0, we have:

𝔼⁡[X]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[X] =μ+ω​𝔼​[Z∣U>0]\displaystyle=\mu+\omega\mathbb{E}[Z\mid U>0] (16)
=μ+ω​𝔼​[𝔼⁡[Z∣U]∣U>0]\displaystyle=\mu+\omega\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Z\mid U]\mid U>0]
=μ+ω([𝔼[Z−Uδ]+𝔼[Uδ∣U>0])\displaystyle=\mu+\omega\left([\mathbb{E}[Z-U\delta]+\mathbb{E}[U\delta\mid U>0]\right)
=μ+𝔼⁡[U∣U>0]⋅ω​δ\displaystyle=\mu+\mathbb{E}[U\mid U>0]\cdot\omega\delta
=μ+2π⋅ω​δ.\displaystyle=\mu+\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\cdot\omega\delta.

If α=ω​R​S−1​k\alpha=\omega RS^{-1}k, associated with Eq.(14), we have:

𝔼⁡[X]=μ+2π⋅R​S​k1+k⊤​k\mathbb{E}[X]=\mu+\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\cdot\frac{RSk}{\sqrt{1+k^{\top}k}} (17)

Appendix B Backward Pass

The learnable parameters for each component in SNS include the location μ\mu, scale matrix Ω\Omega(i.e.i.e. SS and RR), color cc, opacity oo, skew kk, and the key gradients are ∂L∂μ\frac{\partial L}{\partial\mu}, ∂L∂S\frac{\partial L}{\partial S}, ∂L∂R\frac{\partial L}{\partial R}, ∂L∂c\frac{\partial L}{\partial c}, ∂L∂o\frac{\partial L}{\partial o}, ∂L∂k\frac{\partial L}{\partial k}, where LL is the loss. LL is calculated between the ground-truth pixel colors and rendered colors. The rendered pixel colors are:

C⁡(u)=∑i=1Nci​ai​(u)​∏j=1i−1(1−aj​(u)),C(u)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}c_{i}a_{i}(u)\prod_{j=1}^{i-1}\left(1-a_{j}(u)\right), (18)

where a⁡(u)=o⋅S​N2​D​(u)a(u)=o\cdot SN^{2D}(u) and u denotes pixel coordinate in 2D images.

Previous methods, such as 3DGS and SSS, compute the gradients with respect to the shape parameters (RR, SS) by first calculating ∂L∂(Ω−1)\frac{\partial L}{\partial(\Omega^{-1})} and subsequently backpropagating to obtain ∂L∂R\frac{\partial L}{\partial R} and ∂L∂S\frac{\partial L}{\partial S}. However, recalling the definitions in Eq. (5) and Eq. (6), computing ∂L∂Ω\frac{\partial L}{\partial\Omega} directly proves cumbersome. The parameters (RR, SS) couple intricately within both A​R​S​kARSk and (Ω2​D)−1(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}, leading to high computational complexity. To mitigate this, we propose an alternative differentiation scheme. By introducing an intermediate variable Q=A​R​SQ=ARS, we reformulate Eq. (5) and Eq. (6) as follows:

S​N2​D​(u)=G2​(u−μ2​D,Q​Q⊤)​Φ​((m2​D)⊤​(u−μ2​D)),SN^{2D}(u)=G_{2}(u-\mu^{2D};QQ^{\top})\,\Phi\left((m^{2D})^{\top}(u-\mu^{2D})\right), (19)

where

m2​D=(Q​Q⊤)−1​Q​k1+k⊤​k−k⊤​Q⊤​(Q​Q⊤)−1​Q​k.m^{2D}=\frac{(QQ^{\top})^{-1}Qk}{\sqrt{1+k^{\top}k-k^{\top}Q^{\top}(QQ^{\top})^{-1}Qk}}.

Applying the chain rule, the gradients are given by:

∂L∂c\displaystyle\frac{\partial L}{\partial c} =∂L∂C⋅∂C∂c,\displaystyle=\frac{\partial L}{\partial C}\cdot\frac{\partial C}{\partial c}, (20)
∂L∂o\displaystyle\frac{\partial L}{\partial o} =∂L∂C⋅∂C∂a⋅∂a∂o,\displaystyle=\frac{\partial L}{\partial C}\cdot\frac{\partial C}{\partial a}\cdot\frac{\partial a}{\partial o},
∂L∂μ\displaystyle\frac{\partial L}{\partial\mu} =∂L∂C⋅∂C∂a⋅∂a∂S​N2​D⋅∂S​N2​D∂μ2​D⋅∂μ2​D∂μ,\displaystyle=\frac{\partial L}{\partial C}\cdot\frac{\partial C}{\partial a}\cdot\frac{\partial a}{\partial SN^{2D}}\cdot\frac{\partial SN^{2D}}{\partial\mu^{2D}}\cdot\frac{\partial\mu^{2D}}{\partial\mu},
∂L∂k\displaystyle\frac{\partial L}{\partial k} =∂L∂C⋅∂C∂a⋅∂a∂S​N2​D⋅∂S​N2​D∂k,\displaystyle=\frac{\partial L}{\partial C}\cdot\frac{\partial C}{\partial a}\cdot\frac{\partial a}{\partial SN^{2D}}\cdot\frac{\partial SN^{2D}}{\partial k},
∂L∂R\displaystyle\frac{\partial L}{\partial R} =∂L∂C⋅∂C∂a⋅∂a∂S​N2​D⋅∂S​N2​D∂Q⋅∂Q∂R,\displaystyle=\frac{\partial L}{\partial C}\cdot\frac{\partial C}{\partial a}\cdot\frac{\partial a}{\partial SN^{2D}}\cdot\frac{\partial SN^{2D}}{\partial Q}\cdot\frac{\partial Q}{\partial R},
∂L∂S\displaystyle\frac{\partial L}{\partial S} =∂L∂C⋅∂C∂a⋅∂a∂S​N2​D⋅∂S​N2​D∂Q⋅∂Q∂S,\displaystyle=\frac{\partial L}{\partial C}\cdot\frac{\partial C}{\partial a}\cdot\frac{\partial a}{\partial SN^{2D}}\cdot\frac{\partial SN^{2D}}{\partial Q}\cdot\frac{\partial Q}{\partial S},

where CC and aa are defined in Eq. (18). Compared to the standard gradient computation in 3DGS, our formulation solely requires deriving the partial derivatives of S​N2​DSN^{2D} with respect to μ2​D\mu^{2D}, kk, and QQ; the gradients for all other standard components remain unchanged and are therefore omitted. The final analytical expressions for these specific derivatives are presented in Eq. (25), Eq. (28), and Eq. (38), respectively. For notational simplicity, we denote m=m2​Dm=m^{2D}, Δ=u−μ2​D\Delta=u-\mu^{2D}, and D=1+k⊤​k−k⊤​Q⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​Q​kD=\sqrt{1+k^{\top}k-k^{\top}Q^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}Qk}. Also, we define the following auxiliary variables:

𝒄Δ\displaystyle\bm{c}_{\Delta} =Φ⋅G2⋅(Ω2​D)−1​Δ,\displaystyle=\Phi\cdot G_{2}\cdot(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\Delta, (21)
𝑴Δ\displaystyle\bm{M}_{\Delta} =Φ⋅G2⋅((Ω2​D)−1​Δ)​((Ω2​D)−1​Δ)⊤,\displaystyle=\Phi\cdot G_{2}\cdot\left((\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\Delta\right)\left((\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\Delta\right)^{\top},
sΔ\displaystyle s_{\Delta} =G22​π​exp⁡(−12​(m⊤​Δ)2),\displaystyle=\frac{G_{2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(m^{\top}\Delta)^{2}\right),
𝒑Δ\displaystyle\bm{p}_{\Delta} =G22​π​exp⁡(−12​(m⊤​Δ)2)⋅(Ω2​D)−1​Δ,\displaystyle=\frac{G_{2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(m^{\top}\Delta)^{2}\right)\cdot(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\Delta,

where sΔ∈ℝs_{\Delta}\in\mathbb{R}, 𝒄Δ,𝒑Δ∈ℝ2\,\bm{c}_{\Delta},\bm{p}_{\Delta}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} and 𝑴Δ∈ℝ2×2\bm{M}_{\Delta}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}.

Gradient with respect to μ2​D\mu^{2D}.

First, we derive the gradient with respect to the mean vector μ2​D\mu^{2D}. Applying the product rule, we obtain:

∂S​N2​D∂μ2​D=Φ⋅∂G2∂μ2​D+G2⋅∂Φ∂μ2​D.\frac{\partial SN^{2D}}{\partial\mu^{2D}}=\Phi\cdot\frac{\partial G_{2}}{\partial\mu^{2D}}+G_{2}\cdot\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial\mu^{2D}}. (22)

Given Δ=u−μ2​D\Delta=u-\mu^{2D}, the inner derivative is ∂Δ∂μ2​D=−I\frac{\partial\Delta}{\partial\mu^{2D}}=-I. So the derivative of the Gaussian component G2G_{2} is:

∂G2∂μ2​D=G2​(Ω2​D)−1​(u−μ2​D)=G2​(Ω2​D)−1​Δ.\frac{\partial G_{2}}{\partial\mu^{2D}}=G_{2}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}(u-\mu^{2D})=G_{2}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\Delta. (23)

For the cumulative distribution function (CDF) component Φ⁡(m⊤​Δ)\Phi(m^{\top}\Delta), the chain rule yields:

∂Φ⁡(m⊤​Δ)∂μ2​D=−12​π​exp⁡(−12​(m⊤​Δ)2)​m.\frac{\partial\Phi(m^{\top}\Delta)}{\partial\mu^{2D}}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(m^{\top}\Delta)^{2}\right)m. (24)

Substituting these partial derivatives back into the product rule and utilizing the definitions in Eq. (21), we arrive at the intermediate expression:

∂S​N2​D∂μ2​D\displaystyle\frac{\partial SN^{2D}}{\partial\mu^{2D}} =Φ⋅G2​(Ω2​D)−1​Δ−G22​π​exp⁡(−12​(m⊤​Δ)2)​m\displaystyle=\Phi\cdot G_{2}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\Delta-\frac{G_{2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(m^{\top}\Delta)^{2}\right)m (25)
=𝒄Δ−sΔ⋅m.\displaystyle=\bm{c}_{\Delta}-s_{\Delta}\cdot m.

Gradient with respect to kk.

Next, we derive the gradient with respect to kk:

∂S​N2​D∂k\displaystyle\frac{\partial SN^{2D}}{\partial k} =G2⋅∂Φ∂(m⊤​Δ)⋅∂(m⊤​Δ)∂k\displaystyle=G_{2}\cdot\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial(m^{\top}\Delta)}\cdot\frac{\partial(m^{\top}\Delta)}{\partial k} (26)
=G22​π​exp⁡(−12​(m⊤​Δ)2)⋅∂(m⊤​Δ)∂k,\displaystyle=\frac{G_{2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(m^{\top}\Delta)^{2}\right)\cdot\frac{\partial(m^{\top}\Delta)}{\partial k},

where

∂(m⊤​Δ)∂k=\displaystyle\frac{\partial(m^{\top}\Delta)}{\partial k}= 1D⋅∂(Δ⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​Q​k)∂k\displaystyle\frac{1}{D}\cdot\frac{\partial\left(\Delta^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}Qk\right)}{\partial k} (27)
−Δ⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​Q​k2​D3⋅∂(k⊤​k−k⊤​Q⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​Q​k)∂k\displaystyle-\frac{\Delta^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}Qk}{2D^{3}}\cdot\frac{\partial\left(k^{\top}k-k^{\top}Q^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}Qk\right)}{\partial k}
=\displaystyle= Q⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​ΔD−Δ⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​Q​kD3⋅(k−Q⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​Q​k)\displaystyle\frac{Q^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\Delta}{D}-\frac{\Delta^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}Qk}{D^{3}}\cdot\left(k-Q^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}Qk\right)
=\displaystyle= Q⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​ΔD+(Δ⊤​m)⋅Q⊤​mD−(Δ⊤​m)⋅kD2\displaystyle\frac{Q^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\Delta}{D}+\frac{(\Delta^{\top}m)\cdot Q^{\top}m}{D}-\frac{(\Delta^{\top}m)\cdot k}{D^{2}}
=\displaystyle= 1D​Q⊤​((Ω2​D)−1​Δ+(Δ⊤​m)⋅m)−1D2⋅(Δ⊤​m)⋅k.\displaystyle\frac{1}{D}Q^{\top}\left((\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\Delta+(\Delta^{\top}m)\cdot m\right)-\frac{1}{D^{2}}\cdot(\Delta^{\top}m)\cdot k.

Combining Eq. (21), Eq. (26), and Eq. (27), we obtain:

∂S​N2​D∂k\displaystyle\frac{\partial SN^{2D}}{\partial k} =1D​Q⊤​(𝒑Δ+(𝒑Δ⊤​Ω2​D​m)⋅m)−1D2⋅(𝒑Δ⊤​Ω2​D​m)⋅k.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{D}Q^{\top}\left(\bm{p}_{\Delta}+(\bm{p}_{\Delta}^{\top}\Omega^{2D}m)\cdot m\right)-\frac{1}{D^{2}}\cdot(\bm{p}_{\Delta}^{\top}\Omega^{2D}m)\cdot k. (28)

Gradient with respect to QQ.

To compute ∂S​N2​D∂Q\frac{\partial SN^{2D}}{\partial Q}, we apply the product rule to the respective terms:

∂S​N2​D∂Q=G2⋅∂Φ∂(m⊤​Δ)⋅∂(m⊤​Δ)∂Q+Φ⋅∂G2∂Q.\displaystyle\frac{\partial SN^{2D}}{\partial Q}=G_{2}\cdot\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial(m^{\top}\Delta)}\cdot\frac{\partial(m^{\top}\Delta)}{\partial Q}+\Phi\cdot\frac{\partial G_{2}}{\partial Q}. (29)

First, we calculate the gradient of the 2D Gaussian G2G_{2} with respect to QQ. The differential of G2G_{2} can be expressed using the trace operator Tr​(⋅)\text{Tr}(\cdot):

d​G2\displaystyle dG_{2} =G2⋅(−12​Δ⊤​d​(Ω2​D)−1​Δ)\displaystyle=G_{2}\cdot\left(-\frac{1}{2}\Delta^{\top}d(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\Delta\right) (30)
=12​G2​Tr​(Δ⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​(Q​d​Q⊤+d​Q​Q⊤)​(Ω2​D)−1​Δ)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}G_{2}\text{Tr}\left(\Delta^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}(QdQ^{\top}+dQQ^{\top})(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\Delta\right)
=Tr​(G2⋅Q⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​Δ​Δ⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​d​Q).\displaystyle=\text{Tr}\left(G_{2}\cdot Q^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\Delta\Delta^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}dQ\right).

By the matrix calculus identity where the differential d​f=Tr​(P⊤​d​Q)df=\text{Tr}(P^{\top}dQ) implies the gradient ∂f∂Q=P\frac{\partial f}{\partial Q}=P, we extract the derivative with respect to QQ:

∂G2∂Q=G2​((Ω2​D)−1​Δ​Δ⊤​(Ω2​D)−1)​Q.\frac{\partial G_{2}}{\partial Q}=G_{2}\left((\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\Delta\Delta^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\right)Q. (31)

Next, we compute ∂(m⊤​Δ)∂Q\frac{\partial(m^{\top}\Delta)}{\partial Q}. Let N=Δ⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​Q​kN=\Delta^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}Qk, which implies m⊤​Δ=NDm^{\top}\Delta=\frac{N}{D}. By the quotient rule, its differential is:

d⁡(m⊤​Δ)=1D​d​N−ND2​d​D=1D​d​N−m⊤​ΔD​d​D.d(m^{\top}\Delta)=\frac{1}{D}dN-\frac{N}{D^{2}}dD=\frac{1}{D}dN-\frac{m^{\top}\Delta}{D}dD. (32)

For d​NdN, evaluating the differential and substituting (Ω2​D)−1​Q​k=D​m(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}Qk=Dm, we have:

d​N\displaystyle dN =Δ⊤​d​((Ω2​D)−1)​Q​k+Δ⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​d​Q​k\displaystyle=\Delta^{\top}d\left((\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\right)Qk+\Delta^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}dQ\,k (33)
=−Δ⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​(d​Q​Q⊤+Q​d​Q⊤)​(Ω2​D)−1​Q​k+Δ⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​d​Q​k\displaystyle=-\Delta^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}(dQ\,Q^{\top}+Q\,dQ^{\top})(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}Qk+\Delta^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}dQ\,k
=Tr​(k​Δ⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​d​Q−Q⊤​D​m​Δ⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​d​Q−D​m​Δ⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​Q​d​Q⊤)\displaystyle=\text{Tr}\left(k\Delta^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}dQ-Q^{\top}Dm\Delta^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}dQ-Dm\Delta^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}QdQ^{\top}\right)
=Tr​([(Ω2​D)−1​Δ​k⊤−D​(Ω2​D)−1​Δ​m⊤​Q−D​m​Δ⊤​(Ω2​D)−1​Q]⊤​d​Q).\displaystyle=\text{Tr}\left(\left[(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\Delta k^{\top}-D(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\Delta m^{\top}Q-Dm\Delta^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}Q\right]^{\top}dQ\right).

This establishes the gradient of NN:

∂N∂Q=(Ω2​D)−1​Δ​k⊤−D⁡((Ω2​D)−1​Δ​m⊤+m​Δ⊤​(Ω2​D)−1)​Q.\frac{\partial N}{\partial Q}=(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\Delta k^{\top}-D\left((\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\Delta m^{\top}+m\Delta^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\right)Q. (34)

Similarly, we derive variable DD’s differential:

d​D\displaystyle dD =−12​D⋅d(k⊤Q⊤(Ω2​D)−1Qk)\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2D}\cdot d\left(k^{\top}Q^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}Qk\right) (35)
=−1D⋅(k⊤Q⊤(Ω2​D)−1dQk−k⊤Q⊤(Ω2​D)−1dQQ⊤(Ω2​D)−1Qk)\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{D}\cdot\left(k^{\top}Q^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}dQ\,k-k^{\top}Q^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}dQ\,Q^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}Qk\right)
=−1D⋅(Dm⊤dQk−D2m⊤dQQ⊤m)\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{D}\cdot\left(Dm^{\top}dQ\,k-D^{2}m^{\top}dQ\,Q^{\top}m\right)
=Tr​((−m​k⊤+D⋅m​m⊤​Q)⊤​d​Q),\displaystyle=\text{Tr}\left(\left(-mk^{\top}+D\cdot mm^{\top}Q\right)^{\top}dQ\right),

which yields:

∂D∂Q=−m​k⊤+D⋅m​m⊤​Q.\frac{\partial D}{\partial Q}=-mk^{\top}+D\cdot mm^{\top}Q. (36)

Combining Eq. (32), Eq. (34), and Eq. (36), we assemble ∂(m⊤​Δ)∂Q\frac{\partial(m^{\top}\Delta)}{\partial Q}:

∂(m⊤​Δ)∂Q=\displaystyle\frac{\partial(m^{\top}\Delta)}{\partial Q}= 1D​((Ω2​D)−1​Δ+(m⊤​Δ)​m)​k⊤\displaystyle\frac{1}{D}\left((\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\Delta+(m^{\top}\Delta)m\right)k^{\top} (37)
−((Ω2​D)−1​Δ​m⊤+m​Δ⊤​(Ω2​D)−1+(m⊤​Δ)​m​m⊤)​Q.\displaystyle-\left((\Omega^{2D})^{-1}\Delta m^{\top}+m\Delta^{\top}(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}+(m^{\top}\Delta)mm^{\top}\right)Q.

Finally, recalling that G2⋅∂Φ∂(m⊤​Δ)=G22​π​exp⁡(−12​(m⊤​Δ)2)G_{2}\cdot\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial(m^{\top}\Delta)}=\frac{G_{2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(m^{\top}\Delta)^{2}\right), we multiply Eq. (37) by this term. Substituting the previously defined variables 𝒑Δ\bm{p}_{\Delta} and MΔM_{\Delta}, the full analytical gradient ∂S​N2​D∂Q\frac{\partial SN^{2D}}{\partial Q} is derived as:

∂S​N2​D∂Q=\displaystyle\frac{\partial SN^{2D}}{\partial Q}= (𝑴Δ−𝒑Δ​m⊤−m​𝒑Δ⊤−(𝒑Δ⊤​Ω2​D​m)⋅m​m⊤)​Q\displaystyle\left(\bm{M}_{\Delta}-\bm{p}_{\Delta}m^{\top}-m\bm{p}_{\Delta}^{\top}-(\bm{p}_{\Delta}^{\top}\Omega^{2D}m)\cdot mm^{\top}\right)Q (38)
+1D​(𝒑Δ+(𝒑Δ⊤​Ω2​D​m)⋅m)​k⊤.\displaystyle+\frac{1}{D}\left(\bm{p}_{\Delta}+(\bm{p}_{\Delta}^{\top}\Omega^{2D}m)\cdot m\right)k^{\top}.

Following the standard 3DGS architecture, the backward pass consists of rendering and preprocessing stages. In standard 3DGS, the rendering stage first computes gradients with respect to 2D image-space variables (e.g., ∂L∂μ2​D\frac{\partial L}{\partial\mu^{2D}} and ∂L∂(Ω2​D)−1\frac{\partial L}{\partial(\Omega^{2D})^{-1}}), and the preprocessing stage uses these intermediate gradients to compute the gradients for 3D learnable parameters.

By contrast, the SNS rendering stage directly evaluates the shared auxiliary terms (𝒄Δ,𝑴Δ,sΔ,𝒑Δ\bm{c}_{\Delta},\bm{M}_{\Delta},s_{\Delta},\bm{p}_{\Delta}), which are intermediate algebraic quantities rather than derivatives. Next, the preprocessing stage leverages these precomputed terms to efficiently evaluate the exact gradients of the 3D parameters using our derived closed-form expressions (Eq. (25), Eq. (28), and Eq. (38)). By algebraically restructuring the complex gradient derivation into clear and concise computations, this formulation maximizes variable reuse and ensures a smooth and efficient computational flow.

Appendix C Detailed results

In this section, we present the detailed results. Specifically, Table 4 reports the complete PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS metrics for our full SNS model and its ablations across all evaluated scenes.

Appendix D Alternating Optimization Strategy

Jointly optimizing the base geometric attributes (rotation and scaling) with the skewness parameters can lead to optimization instability due to their highly coupled influence on the primitive’s spatial footprint. To mitigate this, we introduce an Alternating Optimization strategy inspired by Block Coordinate Descent (BCD).

As outlined in Algorithm 1, we partition the shape-related parameters into two disjoint groups: the base shape parameters Θb​a​s​e={R,S}\Theta_{base}=\{R,S\} and the skewness parameters Θs​k​e​w={dk,mk}\Theta_{skew}=\{d_{k},m_{k}\}. During the initial warm-up phase (before iteration Ts​t​a​r​tT_{start}), all parameters are optimized jointly to establish a reasonable geometry. Once the threshold Ts​t​a​r​tT_{start} is reached, we interleave the optimization of Θb​a​s​e\Theta_{base} and Θs​k​e​w\Theta_{skew} within a fixed cycle length CC. In each cycle, we freeze the skewness to refine the base shape for Cb​a​s​eC_{base} steps, and subsequently freeze the base shape to optimize the skewness for the remaining steps. This decoupled optimization stabilizes the gradient descent and prevents degenerate primitive shapes.

Appendix E Limitations and future work.

While SNS improves the reconstruction of asymmetric geometries and sharp boundaries, it introduces certain limitations. First, evaluating the Skew-Normal distribution requires computing the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF). In our current implementation, we directly employ the highly accurate numerical solution (the erf function) to ensure mathematical precision. While faster analytic approximations exist, relying on the precise erf incurs moderate penalties on rendering speed. Second, as SNS primarily enhances geometric representation, it still shares the limitations of 3DGS in modeling highly specular surfaces using Spherical Harmonics (SH). Third, as observed in our ablation studies, while the full combined model achieves the highest average PSNR, individual variants slightly outperform it on SSIM and LPIPS. This reveals that a consistently optimal optimization method that uniformly maximizes all evaluation metrics has not been found.

Future work will focus on reducing the CDF computational overhead and exploring more comprehensive optimization algorithms to jointly improve both reconstruction fidelity and perceptual quality. Furthermore, rather than applying complex asymmetric kernels globally, we plan to integrate SNS with spatial hierarchical structures. This would allow the model to adaptively allocate Skew-Normal primitives along high-frequency object boundaries while falling back to simpler Gaussians in smooth regions, thereby optimizing the overall efficiency-to-quality trade-off.
